2.text: perform his last journey: therefore he had, perforce, to renounce the use of

3.text: reindeer on this occasion. The description continues, —

4.text: “Then they asked the corpse, ‘How do you wish to go away? Do you

5.text: want to take a team?’ But the dead man answered, ‘No!’ They asked him,

6.text: ‘Maybe you want to walk?’ He said, ‘I will walk, but you must give me a

7.text: walking-staff.’” Of course, the last answer was procured by means of divination.

8.text: In another relation of a similar kind, the narrator ventured to express

9.text: his severe disapproval of the stinginess of those among the dead who would

10.text: grudge a poor man a few clothes borrowed from their successors.¹

11.text: A person who has several teams is asked about them one by one, and

12.text: the choice between them is determined in the way described above. The

13.text: corpse is often asked also about the man who will direct his reindeer on the

14.text: last journey, and thus be the leader of the funeral cortege, and also about

15.text: an extra “fortifier” to be invited. Then the questioner proceeds to inquire the

16.text: cause of the death and of means warding off further attacks by the keˊlet.

17.text: The future fate of every person present is also made the subject of inquiry,

18.text: as is described in another account of this kind: —

19.text: “They ask the corpse, ‘Will the disease come again afterward?’ and then

20.text: they draw the stick. The corpse answers, ‘The disease will not come back,

21.text: the evil state of things.’ — ‘Tell us plainly about all those standing around,

22.text: whether to any of them there will happen some evil or misfortune. Tell it

23.text: of them one by one.’ If, while they ask about some one of the bystanders,

24.text: the weight is light in drawing, that one will surely die soon.”²

25.text: Then follow questions concerning the coming fortune of the herd, about

26.text: the hunting-pursuits, etc. For instance, in a case I mentioned before, the

27.text: husband proceeded personally to question his deceased wife. He lifted

28.text: the stick which supported by a strap the head of the dead body, and

29.text: began with the divination. His first question was, “What place do you

30.text: want to choose for your funeral?” But the body was as heavy and motionless

31.text: as ever. “Oh!” said the old man, “my mind is not very strong: perhaps I

32.text: offended you with something. You must not hold ill-will to me. You know

33.text: that you have to go away.” But the body obstinately refused to answer.

34.text: “Perhaps you are angry,” said the old man, “that I brought you here from

35.text: Chaun; but this is your own country, the mountains and the rivers all are

36.text: your own. It is quite becoming that you should lie here.”³ But the body

37.text: was motionless, as before. “Alas!” complained the old man, “I am sure you

38.text: are angry. Now I see that you have sent us this snow-storm because your

39.text: mind is not at rest.” [The snow was falling thick outside of the tent.] His
